prompt:

   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?

   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?

   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?

   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?

   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?

   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Quanta is the top dog in a fast-growing, important industry (grid and data-center power infrastructure) with strong past price appreciation (about +353% over five years) and a common 'overvalued' label, which fit Rule Breaker traits. It falls short on consumer brand and on a hard-to-copy innovation advantage, since it is a contractor rather than a product innovator.
summaries.buffett: Quanta is simple to understand, consistently profitable for at least ten years and generates more free cash flow than net income, but its moat is moderate, returns on capital are around 10-15%, debt exceeds cash, and at about 65x trailing earnings the price offers no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the essential, durable demand for grid work and the scale advantage in skilled labor, but thin 5.7% operating margins, an acquisition-heavy growth model and a premium valuation make it a fair business at a full price rather than a great business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: Quanta is a clear fast grower with a simple story (more electricity demand needs more grid construction), but with a trailing P/E near 65 and a forward P/E around 30 against roughly 17-20% expected EPS growth, it fails Lynch's P/E-to-growth test, and it is widely followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Quanta has a long sales runway, strong customer relationships and an execution-focused management team that keeps adding capabilities (data-center electrical, fabrication, engineering, circuit breakers), but as a services firm it has little R&D and only average profit margins, so it meets some but not all of Fisher's points.
summaries.graham: Quanta is large and has been profitable every year from 2016 to 2025 with EPS rising from $1.59 (2015) to $6.80 (2025), but it has paid dividends only since late 2018 and trades at about 65x earnings and 8.8x book, far outside Graham's defensive limits.
summaries.thiel: Quanta has no proprietary technology that is ten times better; its edge is scale, labor and distribution with utilities. Timing is excellent given AI-driven load growth, and its position looks durable, but it is not a monopoly built on a secret.
summaries.gerstner: Quanta is a leading beneficiary of the AI and electrification build-out, with revenue up 41% in Q2 2026 and guidance raised to $39.3-39.7 billion, which fits Gerstner's focus on durable growth. Its thin margins and roughly 30x forward P/E with a PEG near 1.5 make it less compelling on his 'growth at a reasonable price' and efficiency lens.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings and estimates are accelerating (2026 adjusted EPS guidance raised to $16.45-16.95 from $13.55-14.25) and a record $53.4 billion backlog supports the next 18-24 months, a setup Druckenmiller likes. The stock's 15% one-month drop and valuation sensitivity to the AI capex cycle argue for caution on sizing.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith seeks high returns on capital, high gross margins and low capital needs; Quanta's ~15% gross margin, ~10% ROIC and acquisition-driven growth fall short of his quality bar, and the valuation is not cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Quanta scores poorly: its earnings yield is only about 2.2% (EV/EBIT around 45) and return on capital is moderate, so it would not rank near the top.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a good business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high rates; Quanta has strong reinvestment opportunities and capable operators, but returns on capital (about 10% ROIC) are only moderate and growth relies heavily on acquisitions.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai wants simple, low-risk businesses bought at a deep discount; Quanta is simple and durable but trades at a large premium, so there is no 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup.
summaries.wood: Quanta supports the energy and AI infrastructure build-out but is not itself a disruptive-innovation platform with falling unit costs, so it fits Cathie Wood's framework only indirectly as an enabler.
summaries.ackman: Quanta fits Ackman's preference for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating businesses with large barriers to entry in part, but its debt exceeds cash, its moat is moderate and the valuation leaves little room for an activist-style upside.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model fits only partly: Quanta's growing scale funds training and capacity that serve utilities better, but there is little evidence it passes scale savings back to customers in a way that compounds into an unassailable position.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets and great timing; Quanta rides a large market (grid and data-center power) at excellent timing, but it is a mature 1997-founded contractor rather than a startup with breakthrough technology.
summaries.nash: Quanta passes Nash's secular-trend, growth (revenue up 20.3% in 2025 and 34% in H1 2026), earnings-beat and category-score tests (about 85/130), but fails key filters: debt exceeds cash, operating margin is below 20%, insiders are selling during an acquisition spree, and the DCF and PEG (about 1.46) do not support today's price.

momentum.evidence: The stock is up about 24-28% over one year and about 29% year to date (vs about 12% for SPY by Oct 21, 2026), but it has fallen about 13% over six months and 15% in the past month to $563.93.

g4.evidence: CEO Duke Austin has a strong execution record since 2016 and institutions own about 92% of shares, but there is no notable famous investor or strategic backer.

g6.evidence: Commentators such as TIKR and Quiver Quantitative cite valuation concerns, with the stock at roughly 65x trailing and 30x forward earnings, well above peers like MasTec and EMCOR.

simple.evidence: Quanta builds and maintains power lines, substations, pipelines and data-center electrical systems for utilities and other customers, a business a generalist can grasp.

b2.evidence: It was profitable every year 2016-2025 and revenue grew every year from 2021 to 2025, from $12.98 billion to $28.48 billion.

integrity.evidence: Disclosure is clear and guidance has been raised 11 times out of 16 updates since late 2022, but the CEO sold about 156,000 shares in early-to-mid 2026 and capital goes heavily to acquisitions.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions mostly extend its core electrical and infrastructure capabilities (Cupertino Electric, Dynamic Systems, Phalcon, Enerfab), but the deal pace (eight acquisitions in 2025 and four in 2026 for about $1.24 billion) leans toward empire-building.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 10% and ROE about 15% (StockAnalysis, TTM), respectable but not high, with $6.10 billion of debt.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $1.67 billion was 163% of net income of $1.03 billion, and TTM free cash flow reached about $2.29 billion.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings and acquisitions grew revenue from $11.20 billion (2020) to $28.48 billion (2025), and the stock returned about 353% over five years, far more than the earnings retained.

safety.evidence: At about 65x trailing earnings, 8.8x book and a 2.7% FCF yield, the price is well above a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 30 and PEG of about 1.46 look expensive for a contractor with 5.7% operating margins, even with fast growth.

mu5.evidence: Grid demand is durable, but failure paths include a capex slowdown in AI data centers, large fixed-price project losses, wildfire or safety liabilities and acquisition integration problems.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest heavily into acquisitions, training and capacity with a $53.4 billion backlog, but returns on that capital are moderate at about 10% ROIC.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower (revenue up 20.3% in 2025 and 41.1% in Q2 2026) with a simple story: more electricity demand requires more grid construction.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 65 and forward P/E of about 30 are well above expected EPS growth of roughly 17% for 2027.

runway.evidence: Utility grid upgrades, data-center load, power generation and new lines like circuit-breaker manufacturing give a long runway, backed by backlog up 49% year on year to $53.4 billion.

ly7.evidence: Insider transactions in the six months to July 2026 were all sales (CEO about 156,000 shares) and diluted shares rose from 145.2 million (2020) to 152.4 million (Q2 2026).

ly8.evidence: Quanta is widely followed (31 analysts, 'Strong Buy' consensus) as an AI-infrastructure play, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: Management keeps adding new service lines (data-center electrical and mechanical, fabrication, engineering, a circuit-breaker JV with Hyosung HICO), mostly via acquisitions rather than in-house development.

fi3.evidence: Quanta does not report meaningful R&D spending, so its R&D results cannot be assessed.

fi4.evidence: It wins large multi-year utility programs and master service agreements, lifting backlog to a record $53.4 billion, but sales rely on relationships and bidding rather than a distinctive sales machine.

longterm.evidence: Investments in its own lineman college, training center and supply-chain manufacturing show long-term thinking, though management focuses heavily on near-term guidance and EPS.

gr1.evidence: Quanta had $28.48 billion of 2025 revenue, about 69,500 employees and a market value of about $85 billion.

ni10.evidence: Net income attributable to common stock was positive each year 2016-2025, from $198.4 million in 2016 to $1,028.4 million in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Quanta initiated its quarterly cash dividend only in December 2018 (now $0.11 per quarter).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.59 in 2015 to $6.80 in 2025, more than four-fold.

gr6.evidence: The share price of $563.93 is about 65 times trailing earnings, far above 15 times.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 64.5 times P/B of about 8.8 gives about 567, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Quanta's advantage is scale and skilled labor, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: AI data-center load growth, electrification and grid replacement are accelerating now, lifting Q2 2026 revenue 41.1% and backlog 49%.

th3.evidence: It began in 1997 as a roll-up of utility contractors that grew into a large share of North American grid services and is expanding into data-center, generation and equipment markets.

team.evidence: CEO Duke Austin has delivered strong results since 2016, but he is not a founder and the team is a capable operator rather than world-renowned.

th5.evidence: Long-standing master service agreements and relationships with large utilities (top ten customers 30% of 2025 revenue) give it a reliable channel to customers.

durable.evidence: Physical grid work cannot be digitised away and demand looks durable for decades, but contracting is competitive and margins thin, so position strength depends on keeping its labor and scale lead.

th7.evidence: Quanta saw early the convergence of utility and data-center power needs and built a 'solutions' model including manufacturing (Hyosung HICO breaker JV), but peers are pursuing the same trend.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of AI-driven electricity demand and grid modernisation; Technology, Manufacturing and Communications revenue rose from 6% of revenue in 2023 to 13% in 2025.

dr1.evidence: In July 2026 Quanta raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $16.45-16.95 from $13.55-14.25 and revenue guidance to $39.3-39.7 billion from $34.7-35.2 billion.

dr2.evidence: A record $53.4 billion backlog and newly acquired businesses expected to add $1.2-1.4 billion of 2026 revenue point to a stronger business, though much of this is already widely expected.

dr4.evidence: Strong utility and hyperscaler capex supports demand, but higher rates raise utility funding costs and any AI capex slowdown would hurt.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on Oct 29, 2026, backlog conversion of large transmission programs, the Hyosung HICO breaker JV and a new $1 billion buyback authorisation are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Demand visibility is high, but thin margins, a premium valuation and a 15% one-month drawdown make a concentrated position risky.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 15.0% in 2025, typical of contractors rather than a sign of strong pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: The FCF yield is about 2.7% (TTM free cash flow of about $2.29 billion on an $85 billion market value), low for a 5.7%-operating-margin contractor.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 45, an earnings yield of roughly 2.2% on an enterprise value of about $90.9 billion.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback; revenue rose 41.1% in Q2 2026 and the recent share-price drop reflects valuation concerns rather than operating problems.

pa4.evidence: The business is durable and investment grade (Moody's Baa2), but a 65x trailing P/E leaves room for a large, lasting price decline if growth slows.

wo1.evidence: It is a leading builder of energy and AI data-center power infrastructure, but it is a contractor rather than a technology leader in AI or energy storage.

wo2.evidence: Its labor-intensive services do not show rapidly falling unit costs with volume.

wo3.evidence: It combines grid, generation and data-center construction services but not multiple disruptive innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market is growing strongly but is unlikely to be many times larger within five years.

ac3.evidence: It is not a commodity producer, but its demand depends on utility and energy capital spending, which is sensitive to interest rates, regulation and energy prices.

ns1.evidence: Scale funds training (Northwest Lineman College) and capacity that help customers, but there is no clear evidence of passing scale savings back through lower prices.

ns4.evidence: Its growing backlog, manufacturing moves and labor pipeline suggest a stronger position in 10-20 years, but competitors are also scaling up for the same grid build-out.

va2.evidence: It solves a large, painful problem: utilities and data centers need far more grid capacity than existing infrastructure and labor can deliver.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the energy and AI infrastructure trend at the physical grid layer, a business built for power infrastructure rather than retrofitted.

tn2.evidence: The market still often sees it as a utility contractor while it is becoming an integrated 'solutions' provider including engineering, fabrication and equipment manufacturing.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap (about $85 billion) U.S. company, not a commodity producer, airline, startup or Chinese company.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since 2021 and it is profitable, but debt ($6.10 billion) exceeds cash ($0.51 billion), a valid miss for an asset-heavy infrastructure business.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in recent quarters (e.g. $886 million in Q2 2026), but debt has exceeded cash every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 20.3% in 2025 and 34% in the first half of 2026.

tn7.evidence: First-half 2026 revenue growth of 34% plus a 6.1% FCF margin is about 40, but for 2025 it was only about 26 (20.3% growth plus 5.9% FCF margin).

tn8.evidence: In H1 2026 revenue grew 34% while cost of services grew 32.4% and SG&A 29.0%.

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: debt exceeds cash and operating margin (5.7% in 2025) is below 20%.

tn10.evidence: There is no major pending regulatory or legal threat known, but wildfire, safety and project-dispute liabilities are ongoing risks of energized-line work.

tn11.evidence: Quanta provides skilled crews and engineering that help utilities and data centers build and maintain power infrastructure, charging under master service agreements and project contracts; customers choose it for scale and reliability.

tn13.evidence: Score about 85: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest (2.15%) 10, institutions (91.5%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return (+353%) 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2021-2025 and FCF stayed positive, but operating margin was flat (5.5% to 5.7%), FCF fell in 2021 to $246 million, and debt exceeded cash.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 7x and the current ratio 1.10 with liabilities 1.9x equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($20.4 billion) are only about 1.1x liabilities ($18.5 billion).

tn18.evidence: Austin has run Quanta for 10 years with strong growth, but he is not the founder, margins have not expanded much and he has been a seller rather than an open-market buyer.

tn20.evidence: Quanta beat EPS consensus in each of the last eight quarters, including Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $4.24 vs about $3.25 expected.

tn21.evidence: Red flags include an acquisition spree (eight deals in 2025, four in 2026) and heavy insider selling (CEO about $120 million in six months) while the stock ran up.

tn22.evidence: It has $32.9 billion of TTM revenue, solid profits and does not issue shares to fund operations.

tn24.evidence: At a 2.7% FCF yield the price implies many years of roughly 20%+ growth; the company is currently delivering 34-41% revenue growth (helped by acquisitions), but sustaining it is uncertain.

tn25.evidence: With TTM FCF of about $2.29 billion, even 20% annual growth for five years and 4% terminal growth at a 12% discount rate gives about $51 billion of equity value, roughly 60% of today's $85 billion market value.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 30 is above contractor peers and the PEG is about 1.46, above 1.
